title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:
1. Course Description
A robot changes the physical world through motor commands. An incorrect command can cause a collision, so the system must constrain motion as well as predict actions. This course examines how to build, deploy, evaluate, and govern such a system. Teams run a learned policy (SmolVLA or ACT) on the Qualcomm Linux processor of an Arduino UNO Q. An independent STM32 safety governor checks whether to permit each command to a Seeed SO-101 arm. Over fourteen weeks, students derive the arm’s kinematics, train and evaluate its policy, and use their measurements to defend a bounded release decision.

title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:
2. Course at a Glance



Format
Two meetings a week: a 90-minute systems seminar and a 3-hour supervised lab. Six labs, then a three-week capstone. No written exam.


Length
14 teaching weeks


Prerequisites
Programming in Python, basic linear algebra and probability, introductory machine learning, and first-year Newtonian physics. C, operating systems, or control experience helps but is not required; staff provide the baseline firmware and support its extension.


Teams
Two or three students per bench station, with rotating roles


Hardware
One station per team: Arduino UNO Q, SO-101 arm, overhead camera, and separate motor power. See the Station Reference Card.


Workload
Seminar and lab each week, plus reading, analysis, and booked bench time. Credits: TBD


Schedule
Seminar early in the week (Monday or Tuesday), lab later in the week (Thursday or Friday). Times and rooms: TBD

title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:
3. Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

Draw a complete path from sensing to actuation and identify which component proposes, which permits, and which executes each physical action.
Calibrate sensors, measure actuator limits, safe states, and end-to-end latency, and set an operating envelope from those measurements.
Compare a simulation with the real hardware and explain where and why they disagree.
Collect and audit robot demonstrations, train and deploy a learned policy on edge hardware, and compare it with a nonlearned baseline.
Distinguish offline model metrics from physical task outcomes, including recovery, abstention, and incomplete motion.
Build and attack a real-time safety governor, and defend a bounded release or no-release decision with evidence from their experiments.

The twelve competencies on the Competency Card define the skills that staff assess at the bench.
Before week 1. Read the Volume IV reader guide and prerequisites and Chapter 1. The book’s appendices provide optional review material on machine learning, systems, and control. Students are not expected to master the appendices before the course begins.

title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:
4. Weekly Structure
Each week connects a chapter reading to a seminar discussion and a supervised experiment. The reading introduces the principles, the seminar examines their implications, and the lab tests them on the station.
Seminar (early in the week, about 90 minutes). Students complete the assigned reading before the seminar. The instructor poses a physical AI question from that reading, and a rotating team presents a raw trace or failed prediction from its station. The class evaluates what the trace supports and considers alternative explanations. The seminar ends by defining the experiment each team will run in the lab.
Lab (later in the week, about 3 hours). The teaching assistant reviews the station’s safe state, motion limits, and the measurement required that week. Teams then complete the assigned lab part. Each part ends with a checkpoint, an artifact that staff inspect before the team proceeds.
Preparation and records. Before each lab, students record their predictions. After the experiment, teams add the raw trace, measurements, differences from the prediction, and the next planned experiment to their shared notebook. Staff check the notebook at the bench. Its records support the lab deliverables; separate weekly lab reports are not required.

title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:
6. The Capstone
Each team defends a release decision for the system it builds. After establishing a working autonomous loop, the team proposes a task at the end of week 8 and fixes its scope at the end of week 10. During weeks 12–14, teams implement the task, test the system against a peer team’s approved faults, and conduct final trials. Each student then defends the team’s Physical Release Dossier in an individual oral exam. A team that demonstrates with rigorous evidence that its system should not be released can earn full marks. The capstone brief specifies the deliverables.

title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:

Three principles govern grading:

Evidence. A favorable model metric does not compensate for a bypassed safety path or unexplained motion. Staff may require a repair and a repeated trial before a team moves on.
Negative results. A negative result supported by measurements and a sound explanation earns more credit than an unmeasured success.
Individual accountability. Teams submit one system, but each student explains their own measurements and a randomly selected trace at the final defense.

The notebook, seminar participation, and the week-13 rehearsal receive feedback but are not graded separately.

title: Physical AI Systems: Course Syllabus
text:
8. Course Policies
Collaboration. Limited bench hardware requires students to complete lab work in teams. Students may discuss ideas across teams, but each student must be able to explain their team’s work at the final defense.
Use of AI tools. Students may use AI tools without penalty. The notebook or deliverable must identify the tools used and describe how they were used. Each student must explain the work without those tools at the final defense.
Late work and repairs. Each lab depends on earlier results, so delays can prevent a team from completing the next experiment. The following rules govern extensions, repairs, and late milestones:

Equipment failures. A team receives an automatic extension for failures outside its control, such as a failed servo or broken station.
Missed checkpoints. A team may complete a missed checkpoint during booked bench time before the next lab. If the team falls further behind, staff provide the reference artifact so that it can continue.
Repairs. Staff may require a correction and a repeated trial before approving a result. A repair finished within a week earns full credit.
Milestones. Late milestones otherwise lose 10% per day unless the team arranges an extension before the deadline.

Accommodations. Students with approved accommodations should contact the instructor in the first week. Lab assessments require physical demonstrations at the bench. Approved lab accommodations provide extra time for checkpoints and milestones.
Office hours. TBD

title: Physical AISystems
text:
The system
The robot operates through a sense → propose → permit → act → observe → revise loop. Camera observations inform a learned policy, which proposes the next move. An independent microcontroller checks whether to permit that move before the arm executes it. A new observation records the result and informs the next decision.
The proposed station combines a Seeed SO-101 arm, an overhead camera, and an Arduino UNO Q. The UNO Q runs the policy on its Linux processor and checks motor commands on its STM32 microcontroller. Staff qualify the station and provide the baseline firmware before student use.




Camera observations feed a Linux policy; proposals cross an authority boundary to the STM32 governor, which permits bounded motor commands. Measured motion and a new camera image close the loop.


Open the control-loop diagram

The final deliverable is a Physical Release Dossier: the operating envelope, baseline comparisons, raw traces, failure evidence, and a defended release decision. A rigorous decision to withhold release can earn full marks. The competency card defines the skills assessed during the labs.

title: Physical AISystems
text:
The semester
Each week pairs a systems seminar with a supervised hardware studio. Students read the assigned chapter before the seminar and predict the outcome of the lab experiment. During the lab, teams compare that prediction with measured behavior and record the results in a shared notebook. The notebook accumulates evidence for the lab assessments and the final release decision.

  01 · WEEKS 1–4Physical limits and kinematicsTeams measure the arm, derive its kinematics, and compare the digital twin with the hardware.
  02 · WEEKS 5–9Policy training and evaluationTeams evaluate a learned policy, adapt it with recorded demonstrations, and test recovery from disturbances.
  03 · WEEKS 10–14Command checks and releaseTeams build the governor and test its response to declared faults. Each student defends a bounded release decision in the capstone.

The syllabus is the canonical source for weekly readings, checkpoints, assessment, and policies. Meeting times, rooms, credits, and enrollment details will be confirmed by course staff.

title: Physical AISystems
text:
The lab sequence
The Getting Started lab introduces the station. The six labs then develop and evaluate the same physical system:

LAB 01The digital twinTeams measure the arm and test its kinematic model.↗
LAB 02Simulation to real hardwareTeams compare predicted motion with measured motion and explain the differences.↗
LAB 03Learned controlTeams compare a learned policy with the nonlearned baseline.↗
LAB 04Real data and fine-tuningTeams collect demonstrations and measure the effect of policy adaptation.↗
LAB 05Stress-test the loopExperiments measure the effects of action horizons and disturbances on recovery.↗
LAB 06Build and attack the governorFault trials test command permission, freshness, refusal, and governor response.↗

CAPSTONE · PHYSICAL RELEASE DEFENSEA release decision supported by measurementsTeams build a bounded task and exchange approved faults with a peer team. Each student defends the resulting release decision.Capstone brief →

title: Physical AISystems
text:
Tools
The proposed tools support data collection, policy training, and experiments on the reference station. Staff select tested versions and supply starter assets. Qualification of the station determines the required policy and export path.

LeRobot + PyTorch: These tools support demonstration datasets, training, and policy evaluation. Training runs on a workstation, and deployment is evaluated on the edge station.
ACT and SmolVLA: These are candidate learned policies. ACT provides action chunking from images and robot state; SmolVLA adds language conditioning. Their station performance must be qualified.
MuJoCo or PyBullet: Staff have not yet selected the simulator. The twin models the same arm and supports matched simulation and hardware trials.
OpenCV + V4L2: These tools support camera calibration, image acquisition, and camera configuration.
ONNX Runtime / INT8: The proposed edge deployment path requires checks of model export, numerical parity, memory use, and timing.
STM32 C + the qualified Arduino/STM32 toolchain: The governor uses this toolchain to implement deterministic command permission, bounds, and watchdog behavior.

The station reference defines the hardware, wiring, and four action taps. Isaac Sim and Cosmos may support research extensions if staff qualify a suitable experiment.

The course assumes working Python skills, introductory machine learning, basic linear algebra and probability, and first-year Newtonian physics. Prior experience with robot arms or microcontrollers is helpful. Staff provide the baseline firmware and support its extension.
